Changing timing or directions can affect performance even when items stay the same, so standard comparisons may no longer apply.
Correct. Standardized scores depend on specified administration and scoring; accessible changes must follow allowable procedures or be reported as nonstandard.
Teams interpreting results need to know about administration changes, so documentation is essential for accurate and transparent decisions.

items.prompt: A student blends spoken sounds accurately but struggles to segment spoken words into individual phonemes during spelling and decoding. What instructional focus does this error pattern indicate?
choices: Instruction in advanced figurative language such as metaphor and idiom within grade-level poetry.
Longer silent-reading sessions designed to build stamina with self-selected chapter books each day.
Practice locating entries with dictionary guide words to strengthen alphabetical order and reference skills.
Explicit, supported sound segmentation linked to letters once the oral task is understood.
items.rationale: The contrast between blending and segmentation identifies a specific sound-analysis need that can be taught directly and connected to encoding and decoding.
choiceRationales: Figurative language is a comprehension and vocabulary topic, so it does not address the phoneme-level analysis that the error pattern reveals.
Silent-reading stamina does not provide explicit practice in hearing and separating sounds, which is the skill the error pattern indicates is weak.
Dictionary skills support reference use but do not teach a student to isolate and map the individual sounds within spoken words.
Correct. The contrast between blending and segmentation identifies a specific sound-analysis need that can be taught directly and connected to encoding and decoding.

items.prompt: Why use unfamiliar or pseudoword decoding tasks?
choices: Applying sound-letter and word-analysis knowledge without relying on stored familiarity with real words.
Background knowledge of the story topic and the student’s ability to predict events from earlier pages.
Writing organization, including paragraph structure, transitions, and the sequencing of ideas in essays.
Listening comprehension of short passages read aloud by the examiner without any printed text present.
items.rationale: Novel-word tasks can sample generative decoding, but interpretation still requires appropriate language, pattern legality, instruction, and comparison with real-word and spelling evidence.
choiceRationales: Correct. Novel-word tasks can sample generative decoding, but interpretation still requires appropriate language, pattern legality, instruction, and comparison with real-word and spelling evidence.
Pseudowords contain no story or topic, so they cannot measure background knowledge or prediction; they isolate decoding of unfamiliar letter patterns.
Writing organization is a composition skill, whereas pseudoword reading examines whether a student can apply decoding knowledge to new letter strings.
Listening comprehension is measured without print, while pseudoword tasks require reading printed letter strings using sound-letter knowledge.

items.prompt: What can an informal reading inventory contribute?
choices: A single standardized diagnosis that determines the student’s reading disability status without other data.
Descriptive task evidence about accuracy, fluency, and comprehension, combined with more reliable measures.
Proof of an exact independent reading level that remains accurate across texts, genres, and topics.
A replacement for word-level analysis, since passage reading already shows each decoding skill needed.
items.rationale: Passage inventories reveal strategies and errors in context but their level labels and comprehension scores can be unstable; decisions need converging evidence.
choiceRationales: Informal inventories vary in reliability and are not diagnostic instruments, so they cannot determine disability status without broader evaluation.
Correct. Passage inventories reveal strategies and errors in context but their level labels and comprehension scores can be unstable; decisions need converging evidence.
Performance shifts with topic, genre, and background knowledge, so an inventory level is an estimate rather than an exact and stable reading level.
Passage reading mixes many skills, so targeted word-level assessment is still needed to pinpoint specific decoding and spelling needs.

items.prompt: How should spelling errors be analyzed?
choices: Treat the misspelled words as random visual memory failures that do not reveal any spelling pattern.
Assess reading comprehension instead of spelling, since comprehension better explains writing difficulties.
Examine sound representation, conventions, inflected endings, and doubling patterns, not just error counts.
Correct each misspelled word on the paper without identifying which spelling patterns caused the errors.
items.rationale: Feature analysis shows what the learner represents and which phonological, orthographic, syllabic, or morphological patterns need explicit instruction.
choiceRationales: Spelling errors usually reflect specific gaps in sound, pattern, or morpheme knowledge, so treating them as random hides useful instructional evidence.
Comprehension assessment cannot explain spelling errors, which require analysis of how the student represents sounds and morphemes in writing.
Correct. Feature analysis shows what the learner represents and which phonological, orthographic, syllabic, or morphological patterns need explicit instruction.
Correcting words without analysis gives no information about patterns, so instruction cannot target the conventions the student has not learned.

items.prompt: A student meets the grade-level words-correct-per-minute benchmark on an oral-reading-fluency check, yet reads word-by-word with poor phrasing and misses comprehension questions. How should the score be interpreted?
choices: The student is fully fluent because the words-correct-per-minute score meets the grade-level benchmark.
The passage was understood because the student missed very few words during the timed oral reading.
Prosody is unrelated to syntax or meaning, so phrasing problems can be set aside when interpreting scores.
Rate is one indicator; accuracy, prosody, and comprehension show fluent reading is not yet secure.
items.rationale: A fluency decision integrates rate with accuracy, phrasing, expression, difficulty, and understanding rather than using a speed cutoff in isolation.
choiceRationales: A rate benchmark captures speed and accuracy but not phrasing or understanding, so it cannot by itself establish fluent, meaningful reading.
Accurate word reading does not guarantee comprehension, so understanding must be checked directly rather than inferred from few errors.
Prosody reflects how readers group words into meaningful phrases, so phrasing problems can signal difficulty processing syntax and meaning.
Correct. A fluency decision integrates rate with accuracy, phrasing, expression, difficulty, and understanding rather than using a speed cutoff in isolation.

items.prompt: What should a comprehension assessment sample?
choices: Inference, text structure, vocabulary, knowledge, monitoring, and summarizing with accessible texts.
Oral reading speed on grade-level passages, recorded as words read correctly within one timed minute.
Letter-name fluency, measured by how many uppercase and lowercase letters a student names in a minute.
Accuracy in copying a passage by hand, which shows whether the student attended to every printed word.
items.rationale: Comprehension is multidimensional and text dependent; aligned tasks help locate whether language, knowledge, strategic integration, print access, or task demands contribute.
choiceRationales: Correct. Comprehension is multidimensional and text dependent; aligned tasks help locate whether language, knowledge, strategic integration, print access, or task demands contribute.
Oral reading speed reflects fluency rather than comprehension, so it cannot show whether students make inferences or understand text structure.
Letter-name fluency is an early literacy screening measure and says little about how a student constructs meaning from connected text.
Copying measures visual attention and transcription, not understanding, so it cannot sample the components of reading comprehension.

items.prompt: Assessment data show that a student decodes grade-level words accurately and fluently yet struggles to comprehend both listened-to and read texts. How should these oral-language and decoding data guide instruction?
choices: More basic letter-name drills should become the primary focus of the student’s intervention schedule.
Teach vocabulary, syntax, knowledge, and language comprehension directly while maintaining word reading.
Accurate decoding shows that the student’s language comprehension is within the normal expected range.
The student should be moved to harder text without support so language skills develop through challenge.
items.rationale: Comparing listening, word recognition, fluency, and reading comprehension helps separate print-access and language-comprehension contributions.
choiceRationales: When decoding is accurate but understanding is weak, letter-name drills target a skill that is already secure and miss the language-based need.
Correct. Comparing listening, word recognition, fluency, and reading comprehension helps separate print-access and language-comprehension contributions.
Decoding and language comprehension are separate components, so accurate decoding cannot demonstrate that oral language skills are adequate.
Harder text without support increases language demands without teaching vocabulary or syntax, which can deepen comprehension difficulties.

items.prompt: How should a multilingual student's reading errors be evaluated?
choices: Identify a reading disability from English reading errors alone once they persist for several months.
Disregard persistent reading concerns because they are expected for students learning English as a new language.
Gather evidence across languages, contexts, instruction, English development, and response to teaching first.
Translate a normed reading test into the home language and keep using its original standard scores.
items.rationale: Valid differential reasoning distinguishes language difference and developing English from disability using qualified multilingual evidence and converging patterns.
choiceRationales: English errors alone cannot distinguish language development from disability, so conclusions require evidence across languages and instructional history.
Persistent concerns still deserve careful investigation; assuming they reflect language learning can delay needed support for a real difficulty.
Correct. Valid differential reasoning distinguishes language difference and developing English from disability using qualified multilingual evidence and converging patterns.
Translation changes item difficulty and the norm comparison, so original standard scores no longer apply and may misrepresent the student’s skills.

items.prompt: What belongs in a comprehensive dyslexia evaluation?
choices: A single letter-reversal checklist completed by the classroom teacher during one writing observation.
An intelligence–achievement discrepancy, which is required in every evaluation before reaching any conclusion.
Reading comprehension scores by themselves, since comprehension is the defining feature of the condition.
Developmental, instructional, language, decoding, spelling, fluency, and phonological evidence under criteria.
items.rationale: No single measure establishes dyslexia; comprehensive evaluation documents a persistent pattern, impact, context, instruction, strengths, co-occurring factors, and applicable rules.
choiceRationales: Reversals are common in early development and are not diagnostic, so a reversal checklist cannot replace a comprehensive multi-source evaluation.
Discrepancy formulas are not universally required and have known limitations, so evaluation relies on multiple sources under current criteria.
Dyslexia centers on word recognition, decoding, and spelling, so comprehension scores alone cannot identify or rule out the condition.
Correct. No single measure establishes dyslexia; comprehensive evaluation documents a persistent pattern, impact, context, instruction, strengths, co-occurring factors, and applicable rules.

items.prompt: What should a writing sample analysis include?
choices: Transcription, sentences, vocabulary, organization, genre, evidence, revision, and conditions used.
Pen color, neatness of margins, and the overall visual appearance of the finished written product.
Oral reading rate on a grade-level passage, which predicts the quality of the student’s written work.
The number of paragraphs in the sample, counted without analyzing the content or organization of ideas.
items.rationale: Analytic and process evidence separates spelling and handwriting demands from language and composition and identifies teachable patterns.
choiceRationales: Correct. Analytic and process evidence separates spelling and handwriting demands from language and composition and identifies teachable patterns.
Visual appearance says little about the language, organization, and reasoning that writing analysis must examine to plan instruction.
Reading rate is a separate skill and cannot describe how well a student plans, organizes, and expresses ideas in written form.
Counting paragraphs captures length rather than coherence, evidence use, or sentence quality, which are central to analyzing writing.

items.prompt: How should a reading specialist synthesize a case?
choices: Average every available score into one composite, regardless of which constructs each assessment measured.
Compare constructs, tasks, reliability, access, context, and error patterns; state uncertainty and seek resolving evidence.
Choose the lowest result across all measures, since it best represents the student’s true reading needs.
Disregard classroom performance because informal evidence is less precise than standardized assessment.
items.rationale: Case integration explains convergence and conflict, links findings to instruction and function, and avoids false certainty or a list of disconnected scores.
choiceRationales: Averaging scores from different constructs hides meaningful patterns and can produce a number that represents no real skill accurately.
Correct. Case integration explains convergence and conflict, links findings to instruction and function, and avoids false certainty or a list of disconnected scores.
The lowest score may reflect fatigue, access barriers, or a mismatched task, so it should be interpreted in context rather than accepted alone.
Classroom performance shows how skills function in authentic tasks and can confirm or challenge standardized results during case synthesis.

items.prompt: What makes progress-monitoring scores comparable over time?
choices: Each weekly probe should assess a different construct so the team builds a broad profile of the student.
The highest weekly score should replace the overall trend because it shows what the student can achieve.
Measures should sample the same outcome with equivalent forms and consistent administration and scoring.
Comparability matters mainly for norm-referenced tests and is less important for curriculum-based probes.
items.rationale: Growth interpretation depends on technical adequacy and comparable measurement; uncontrolled changes can create score differences unrelated to learning.
choiceRationales: Changing constructs each week prevents a meaningful trend, because scores cannot be compared when they measure different skills.
A single high score may reflect an easier form or a good day, so decisions should rely on the overall trend rather than isolated peaks.
Correct. Growth interpretation depends on technical adequacy and comparable measurement; uncontrolled changes can create score differences unrelated to learning.
Curriculum-based monitoring depends on comparable forms and consistent administration, and without that comparability the growth estimates become unreliable.

items.prompt: How should a baseline be established?
choices: Select the lowest available score as the baseline so later results show the largest possible growth.
Use a score from an unrelated skill area because it is already available in the student’s records.
Wait until the intervention ends to define the baseline so it reflects the student’s final performance.
Use several valid observations or the measure’s baseline procedure to limit one atypical score.
items.rationale: A representative baseline anchors level and growth decisions; multiple observations and standardized procedures reduce random error and reactivity.
choiceRationales: Choosing the lowest score inflates apparent growth and misrepresents the student’s starting point, leading to inaccurate decisions about progress.
A baseline must measure the same skill that will be monitored, so scores from unrelated areas cannot support valid growth comparisons.
A baseline describes performance before the intervention; setting it at the end removes the starting point needed to evaluate change.
Correct. A representative baseline anchors level and growth decisions; multiple observations and standardized procedures reduce random error and reactivity.

items.prompt: What makes a progress goal defensible?
choices: Set a time-bound goal from baseline, outcome expectations, measure guidance, evidence, and team judgment.
Use the same numerical goal for every grade level so goals are easy to compare across the school.
Choose the goal after reviewing the final data so it matches the growth the student actually made.
Base the goal mainly on the student’s stated preference for how much progress feels comfortable.
items.rationale: Goals should be ambitious and attainable enough to guide action, with their rationale, timeline, measure, and decision rules explicit.
choiceRationales: Correct. Goals should be ambitious and attainable enough to guide action, with their rationale, timeline, measure, and decision rules explicit.
Expected growth differs by grade, skill, and measure, so one numerical goal for every grade ignores relevant benchmarks and baseline data.
Setting goals after seeing results removes accountability and prevents the team from judging whether instruction produced adequate progress.
Student input supports ownership, but goals also need baseline data, measure guidance, and expected growth rates to be defensible.

items.prompt: How should level and slope be interpreted together?
choices: Disregard the trend line because the most recent score falls below the goal established for the student.
Current level, growth rate and stability, remaining time, goal fit, fidelity, and diagnostic data.
Declare that the intervention has succeeded after a single score increase between consecutive probes.
Change the outcome measure immediately whenever the level and slope appear to tell different stories.
items.rationale: Level describes current performance and slope describes change; a sound decision uses the full series and preestablished rules rather than one point.
choiceRationales: One low score may reflect normal variability, so the overall trend should be considered rather than a single point below the goal line.
Correct. Level describes current performance and slope describes change; a sound decision uses the full series and preestablished rules rather than one point.
A single increase can occur by chance, so success decisions require a stable pattern of growth relative to the goal over time.
Switching measures prevents comparison with earlier data; differing level and slope information should be interpreted, not discarded.

items.prompt: Why check intervention fidelity before interpreting nonresponse?
choices: Conclude that the student cannot learn the target skill because the planned intervention did not work.
Intensify the current program without reviewing what was actually delivered during the intervention.
Determine whether the planned content, dosage, grouping, and procedures were delivered adequately.
Leave attendance records out of the data discussion because absences are outside instructional control.
items.rationale: Response data cannot be attributed confidently to an intervention that was not implemented as planned; fidelity review precedes causal claims and guides next steps.
choiceRationales: Nonresponse may reflect weak implementation rather than student ability, so fidelity must be checked before drawing conclusions about learning.
Intensifying a program without knowing whether it was delivered as planned may repeat the same implementation problems at higher cost.
Correct. Response data cannot be attributed confidently to an intervention that was not implemented as planned; fidelity review precedes causal claims and guides next steps.
Absences reduce instructional dosage, so attendance is essential context for interpreting whether the student received the planned support.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a phase-change line on a graph?
choices: Remove the earlier data points from the graph so the team can focus attention on the newest scores.
Move the goal line so it matches the student’s most recent score after the instructional change.
Connect only the highest points on the graph so the visual trend highlights the student’s strengths.
Mark when a documented change began so trends before and after it can be interpreted.
items.rationale: Phase-change documentation links decisions with implementation and helps teams evaluate whether a purposeful adaptation is followed by improved performance.
choiceRationales: Earlier data are needed to compare performance before and after the change, so removing them prevents evaluation of the adjustment.
Moving the goal to match current scores lowers expectations and hides whether the instructional change produced adequate growth.
Connecting only high points distorts the trend and misrepresents progress, which leads to inaccurate decisions about instruction.
Correct. Phase-change documentation links decisions with implementation and helps teams evaluate whether a purposeful adaptation is followed by improved performance.

items.prompt: How should a team respond to insufficient progress with adequate fidelity?
choices: Review diagnostic data, form a hypothesis, adapt the plan, document the change, and keep monitoring.
Continue the current plan indefinitely because the intervention was delivered with adequate fidelity.
Switch to an unrelated intervention chosen at random so the student experiences a fresh approach.
End support for the student because the data show low performance despite faithful implementation.
items.rationale: Data-based individualization is an iterative cycle of validated intervention, progress data, diagnostic analysis, purposeful adaptation, and evaluation.
choiceRationales: Correct. Data-based individualization is an iterative cycle of validated intervention, progress data, diagnostic analysis, purposeful adaptation, and evaluation.
Adequate fidelity with insufficient progress shows the plan does not fit the student’s needs, so continuing unchanged wastes instructional time.
Random program changes ignore diagnostic evidence, so they are unlikely to target the specific skill that is limiting the student’s growth.
Low progress signals a need for more intensive or different support, so ending services would leave the student’s needs unaddressed.

items.prompt: How can schoolwide data be used responsibly?
choices: Rank teachers publicly using a single schoolwide reading metric to encourage stronger classroom results.
Investigate opportunity, curriculum, instruction, access, measure fairness, and implementation.
Conclude that a subgroup with lower scores has lower underlying ability and adjust expectations to match.
Hide subgroup score patterns from staff and families so the data do not create unnecessary concern.
items.rationale: Aggregated data can reveal inequities and system needs, but valid improvement requires contextual analysis, disaggregation, stakeholder voice, and multiple evidence sources.
choiceRationales: Public ranking from one metric ignores context and can damage collaboration, while doing little to identify instructional causes of results.
Correct. Aggregated data can reveal inequities and system needs, but valid improvement requires contextual analysis, disaggregation, stakeholder voice, and multiple evidence sources.
Score gaps usually reflect differences in opportunity, instruction, or measure fairness, so attributing them to ability is inaccurate and harmful.
Hiding subgroup patterns prevents the school from addressing inequities and denies families information they need to advocate effectively.

items.prompt: How can students participate in progress monitoring?
choices: Display ranked progress scores for the whole class so students can compare their growth with peers.
Withhold progress data from the student so that low scores do not affect motivation or confidence.
Explain the goal and graph accessibly, celebrate strategy-linked growth, invite reflection, and plan next steps.
Promise the student that greater effort will always produce the same rate of growth on the graph.
items.rationale: Student involvement is strongest when data are understandable, private, connected to controllable strategies, and used for collaborative goal setting.
choiceRationales: Public ranking invites comparison and embarrassment, whereas private, accessible review helps each student understand personal progress and goals.
Students benefit from understanding their own goals and progress, and withholding data removes a chance to build ownership and self-monitoring.
Correct. Student involvement is strongest when data are understandable, private, connected to controllable strategies, and used for collaborative goal setting.
Growth depends on instruction and many other factors, so promising uniform results from effort can lead to discouragement when progress varies.

items.prompt: How should progress data be communicated to families?
choices: Report only the student’s percentile rank so the family receives a single, easily understood number.
Assure the family that the student will reach grade-level performance by the end of the school year.
Share identifiable data from other students so the family can see how their child compares with peers.
Describe the skill, baseline, goal, intervention, trend, uncertainty, decision, and ways the family can contribute.
items.rationale: Accessible communication translates data into the instructional question and next step while protecting privacy and inviting meaningful family partnership.
choiceRationales: A percentile alone omits the skill, goal, trend, and instructional plan, leaving families without the context they need to participate.
Promising specific outcomes overstates certainty and can damage trust if progress varies; communication should describe trends and uncertainty.
Sharing other students’ identifiable data violates privacy expectations and is not necessary to explain a child’s individual progress.
Correct. Accessible communication translates data into the instructional question and next step while protecting privacy and inviting meaningful family partnership.

items.prompt: What is an asset-based approach to multilingual literacy?
choices: Identify linguistic, cultural, and knowledge resources that support English growth while teaching new forms.
Set aside English instructional needs so learners can focus mainly on developing their home language first.
Require students to think and plan in English during literacy tasks so translation habits fade quickly.
Assume that literacy skills transfer identically across all languages without examining specific differences.
items.rationale: Asset-based practice recognizes transferable knowledge and identity while examining language-specific differences, opportunity, explicit instruction, and individual performance.
choiceRationales: Correct. Asset-based practice recognizes transferable knowledge and identity while examining language-specific differences, opportunity, explicit instruction, and individual performance.
An asset-based approach builds on home-language strengths while still providing explicit English instruction, rather than neglecting English needs.
Requiring English-only thinking removes a valuable resource for understanding and planning, which can slow comprehension and composition growth.
Transfer varies with the features of each language, so teachers examine specific similarities and contrasts instead of assuming identical transfer.

items.prompt: How can cross-linguistic analysis support instruction?
choices: Count the cross-language spelling pattern as evidence of a disability that should be referred for evaluation.
Determine whether the pattern reflects predictable transfer, teach the English contrast, and monitor growth.
Disregard the pattern because cross-language influences fade over time without any targeted instruction.
Discourage the student from using both languages so the cross-language influence stops appearing in writing.
items.rationale: Cross-linguistic analysis helps distinguish developing language from persistent difficulty and turns contrastive patterns into explicit instructional opportunities.
choiceRationales: Predictable cross-language patterns are typical of English development and should not be treated as disability evidence without broader data.
Correct. Cross-linguistic analysis helps distinguish developing language from persistent difficulty and turns contrastive patterns into explicit instructional opportunities.
Some influences persist without explicit teaching, so recognizing the pattern and teaching the English contrast supports more accurate spelling.
Discouraging either language removes a resource for learning and does not teach the specific English contrast the student needs to master.

items.prompt: How should teams distinguish language difference from disability?
choices: A single English-only cutoff score applied to every student regardless of language background or schooling history.
The family’s accent, country of origin, or immigration history as described in enrollment records and interviews.
Instruction quality, language development, performance across languages and contexts, and response to teaching.
A translated version of a standardized test that keeps the original English norms for score interpretation.
items.rationale: Differential decisions require converging evidence that difficulty is not explained primarily by language development, culture, instruction, mobility, or access.
choiceRationales: An English-only cutoff cannot separate language development from disability, because it ignores schooling history and performance in other languages.
Accent and immigration history are unrelated to disability and using them as evidence introduces bias into decisions about a student’s needs.
Correct. Differential decisions require converging evidence that difficulty is not explained primarily by language development, culture, instruction, mobility, or access.
Translation changes item difficulty, so original norms no longer apply and may misrepresent the student’s skills during evaluation decisions.

items.prompt: What makes family literacy engagement reciprocal?
choices: Assign one standardized home reading activity to every family so expectations remain consistent across homes.
Judge family engagement mainly by attendance at school events such as open houses and literacy nights.
Ask students to interpret confidential meetings for family members who prefer a language other than English.
Learn family goals, languages, and routines; co-design feasible supports and communicate in preferred ways.
items.rationale: Reciprocal partnership values family expertise and shared decisions rather than treating families as passive implementers of school-selected practices.
choiceRationales: A single required activity ignores differences in family schedules, languages, and literacy practices that can support reading at home.
Event attendance overlooks the many ways families support literacy, such as storytelling, home-language reading, and daily conversation.
Children should not interpret confidential school matters, which requires qualified interpreters to protect accuracy and family privacy.
Correct. Reciprocal partnership values family expertise and shared decisions rather than treating families as passive implementers of school-selected practices.

items.prompt: How should text selection support equity?
choices: Build access to accurate, varied authors, identities, genres, and perspectives while examining stereotypes.
Lower text complexity whenever a selection features cultures that are unfamiliar to most students in the class.
Select classroom texts mainly by their cover images so the library looks diverse to visitors and families.
Avoid texts that present contested perspectives so classroom discussions stay calm and focused on content.
items.rationale: Equitable text systems combine representation, authenticity, quality, access, challenge, and critical examination throughout the curriculum.
choiceRationales: Correct. Equitable text systems combine representation, authenticity, quality, access, challenge, and critical examination throughout the curriculum.
Unfamiliar cultural content can be supported through background building, so lowering complexity reduces rigor without addressing the real need.
Cover images can be misleading, so equitable text selection examines accuracy, authorship, and representation within the actual text itself.
Avoiding varied perspectives limits critical reading, while guided discussion helps students analyze and compare differing viewpoints respectfully and thoughtfully.

items.prompt: How should a specialist support an advanced reader?
choices: Assign additional repetitive worksheets on already mastered skills so the student stays busy during lessons.
Use evidence to offer deeper complexity, inquiry, rich writing, authentic audiences, choice, and help with uneven skills.
Assume that advanced reading ability means the student has no remaining support needs in any literacy area.
Move the student ahead to higher text levels alone without attention to depth, writing, or discussion quality.
items.rationale: Advanced learners benefit from depth, complexity, knowledge, creativity, and responsive pacing, with assessment of strengths and any coexisting needs.
choiceRationales: Extra practice on mastered skills wastes learning time and can reduce motivation for advanced readers who need greater depth and challenge.
Correct. Advanced learners benefit from depth, complexity, knowledge, creativity, and responsive pacing, with assessment of strengths and any coexisting needs.
Advanced readers may still have uneven needs in areas such as writing or spelling, so evidence should guide support across components.
Text level alone does not build depth; advanced readers benefit from complex inquiry, writing, and discussion rather than simply harder books.

items.prompt: What is the role of assistive technology in literacy access?
choices: Score speech-to-text writing as evidence of handwriting fluency on the student’s next progress report.
Withhold the assistive tool from every graded assignment so scores reflect unsupported performance only.
Evaluate the content and composition goals with the support while assessing transcription separately when it is targeted.
Assume the assistive tool generates the student’s ideas, so content scores should be discounted accordingly.
items.rationale: Assistive technology can reduce an access barrier; valid use requires clarity about the construct, instruction in tool use, documentation, and separate measurement when needed.
choiceRationales: Speech-to-text bypasses handwriting, so it cannot provide evidence about handwriting fluency, which must be assessed directly when targeted.
Withholding tools from all graded work limits access to content goals; supports should be used whenever transcription is not the target skill.
Correct. Assistive technology can reduce an access barrier; valid use requires clarity about the construct, instruction in tool use, documentation, and separate measurement when needed.
Speech-to-text records the student’s spoken ideas rather than creating them, so the content still reflects the student’s own thinking.

items.prompt: What should be clarified before a coaching cycle begins?
choices: Begin recording the teacher’s lessons without discussing the purpose so instruction appears natural on video.
Promise the teacher complete confidentiality for every observation regardless of district policy or duties.
Let administrators and the teacher hold different assumptions about whether coaching is evaluative.
Clarify role, purpose, confidentiality limits, goals, data use, authority, and how feedback is shared.
items.rationale: Role clarity and informed agreements build trust and prevent coaching evidence from being used in ways participants did not understand.
choiceRationales: Recording without agreement violates trust and may breach policy; a coaching cycle should begin with transparent purposes and permissions.
Confidentiality has limits set by policy and safety duties, so promising complete secrecy is inaccurate and can damage trust later.
Unclear expectations about evaluation undermine trust and openness, so roles and purposes should be clarified for everyone in advance.
Correct. Role clarity and informed agreements build trust and prevent coaching evidence from being used in ways participants did not understand.

items.prompt: Which set of practices makes literacy coaching genuinely job embedded?
choices: Use collaborative goals, co-planning, modeling or co-teaching, observation, feedback, rehearsal, and student evidence.
Send teachers a generic research article and assume they will translate it into classroom practice.
Wait until the annual evaluation cycle to discuss literacy practice so feedback is formally documented.
Require teachers to implement a new practice without materials, modeling, or opportunities to rehearse.
items.rationale: Job-embedded professional learning connects evidence and explanation with supported enactment, reflection, feedback, and iterative refinement.
choiceRationales: Correct. Job-embedded professional learning connects evidence and explanation with supported enactment, reflection, feedback, and iterative refinement.
Reading an article provides information but not the modeling, practice, and feedback teachers need to apply new strategies in their classrooms.
Annual evaluation is too infrequent and evaluative to support ongoing growth; job-embedded coaching provides timely collaborative feedback.
Implementation without materials or rehearsal sets teachers up for difficulty and reduces the likelihood that new practices are sustained.

items.prompt: When is modeling most effective in coaching?
choices: An unannounced demonstration lesson taught by the coach with no planning conversation or debrief afterward.
A shared focus, explanation of key decisions, observable look-fors, debriefing, teacher rehearsal, and follow-up evidence.
A detailed script that the teacher must copy word for word regardless of the needs of the students present.
Feedback limited to whether the demonstration lesson felt entertaining and engaging for the students.
items.rationale: Modeling supports transfer when the instructional reasoning is visible and the teacher can analyze, practice, adapt, and receive feedback.
choiceRationales: Without shared planning and debriefing, the teacher may not notice the key decisions in the lesson, which limits transfer to their own teaching.
Correct. Modeling supports transfer when the instructional reasoning is visible and the teacher can analyze, practice, adapt, and receive feedback.
Rigid scripts ignore student needs and teacher judgment, so modeling should highlight adaptable decisions rather than exact wording.
Engagement matters, but useful feedback also examines student learning evidence and the specific instructional moves being modeled.

items.prompt: How should professional learning be evaluated?
choices: End-of-session satisfaction ratings, which indicate whether teachers enjoyed and valued the training.
A single student’s improved score after training, which demonstrates that the training caused learning.
Changes in educator knowledge and practice, implementation conditions, student opportunity and outcomes, and side effects.
Attendance records for each session, since participation shows that teachers implemented the practice.
items.rationale: Professional learning evaluation moves beyond reaction to learning, enactment, system support, and relevant student evidence without overclaiming causality.
choiceRationales: Satisfaction ratings show whether participants liked the training but not whether practice changed or student learning improved afterward.
One student’s score cannot establish that training caused improvement, because many other factors influence individual results.
Correct. Professional learning evaluation moves beyond reaction to learning, enactment, system support, and relevant student evidence without overclaiming causality.
Attending training does not ensure implementation, so evaluation needs evidence of changed classroom practice and student outcomes.

items.prompt: What is a constructive response to instructional disagreement?
choices: Adopt the position argued most forcefully during the meeting so the team can reach a decision quickly.
Avoid raising the disagreement until the conflict fades on its own and the team returns to routine work.
Frame the colleague’s disagreement as personal resistance to change rather than examining their evidence.
Define the shared student goal, surface assumptions and evidence, examine data, agree on a testable plan, and review it.
items.rationale: Collaborative conflict resolution preserves relationships while making the instructional question, evidence, decision process, and follow-up explicit.
choiceRationales: Forceful argument is not evidence, so deciding by volume can lead to poor instructional choices and discourage other perspectives.
Unaddressed disagreements often persist and affect instruction, whereas structured discussion of evidence helps the team move forward.
Labeling disagreement as resistance dismisses potentially valid concerns and damages the trust that teams need for collaborative improvement.
Correct. Collaborative conflict resolution preserves relationships while making the instructional question, evidence, decision process, and follow-up explicit.

items.prompt: How do adult-learning principles inform literacy coaching?
choices: Use relevant problems, prior expertise, choice, active practice, feedback, collaboration, and immediate application.
Assume adult learners benefit most from passive compliance with directives delivered in large lectures.
Avoid acknowledging teachers’ existing expertise so that new practices receive full and equal attention.
Separate professional sessions from real classroom problems so teachers can focus on general theory.
items.rationale: Effective adult learning is purposeful, respectful, active, context connected, and supported over time rather than a one-time information delivery.
choiceRationales: Correct. Effective adult learning is purposeful, respectful, active, context connected, and supported over time rather than a one-time information delivery.
Adults learn best when they actively engage with relevant problems; passive compliance rarely produces lasting change in classroom practice.
Building on teachers’ existing expertise increases relevance and trust, while ignoring it can reduce engagement with new practices.
Connecting learning to real classroom problems increases relevance and supports immediate application of new literacy practices.

items.prompt: What makes a literacy data meeting productive?
choices: Add more unrelated dashboards and reports so participants can review as much information as possible.
A focused question, prepared disaggregated evidence, agreed norms, analysis of instruction, and a documented action plan.
Use the meeting to rank teachers by student scores so staff understand where improvement is needed.
End the meeting after discussion without recording decisions so the conversation can stay informal.
items.rationale: A disciplined inquiry cycle turns data into a specific, testable instructional or system action and protects against deficit explanations and meeting drift.
choiceRationales: Extra unrelated data overwhelm participants and pull attention away from a focused question that can guide a concrete instructional decision.
Correct. A disciplined inquiry cycle turns data into a specific, testable instructional or system action and protects against deficit explanations and meeting drift.
Ranking teachers by scores creates defensiveness and undermines collaboration without identifying the specific instructional changes that students need.
Without documented decisions, owners, and review dates, teams cannot follow through on actions or check whether they made a difference.

items.prompt: What is the reading specialist's role in MTSS leadership?
choices: Assign students permanently to intervention tiers based on fall screening results so building schedules and staffing remain stable.
Use tiered intervention as a substitute for special-education evaluation whenever families submit a written request for an evaluation.
Coordinate core instruction, screening, support, monitoring, and teams; tiered support must not delay or deny evaluation.
Make the reading specialist solely responsible for every struggling reader in the school, including planning core classroom instruction.
items.rationale: MTSS is a prevention and support framework involving system quality and increasingly intensive response, not a static placement or reason to delay required evaluation.
choiceRationales: Tier placement should change with progress data; permanent assignment ignores growth and can keep students in support they no longer need.
Federal guidance prohibits using intervention to delay or deny a warranted evaluation, so tiers cannot replace the evaluation process.
Correct. MTSS is a prevention and support framework involving system quality and increasingly intensive response, not a static placement or reason to delay required evaluation.
Supporting struggling readers is a shared responsibility; placing it on one person is unsustainable and weakens core classroom instruction.

items.prompt: How should a literacy program be evaluated?
choices: Vendor testimonials and marketing materials describing results achieved in other districts and schools.
The highest average score earned by a single grade level during the most recent assessment window.
Teacher compliance with the program schedule, measured without reference to student learning evidence.
Implementation, component outcomes, growth, subgroup access, educator learning, coherence, and unintended effects.
items.rationale: Program evaluation examines whether the design was enacted, for whom it worked, under what conditions, and what should be sustained, adapted, or discontinued.
choiceRationales: Vendor testimonials are not independent evidence and may not reflect local implementation, students, or outcomes in the current setting.
One grade’s top score cannot represent overall program effectiveness, which requires evidence across grades, components, and subgroups.
Compliance shows that a program was used but not whether students benefited, so evaluation must include student outcome evidence.
Correct. Program evaluation examines whether the design was enacted, for whom it worked, under what conditions, and what should be sustained, adapted, or discontinued.

items.prompt: How should leaders select literacy materials or programs?
choices: Independent evidence and fit, instructional design, alignment, population, implementation demands, access, and cost.
Choose the most colorful and visually appealing materials so students feel motivated to use them daily.
Treat a long list of research citations in the vendor brochure as proof that the program is effective.
Disregard local staffing capacity and learner profiles because strong programs work in every setting.
items.rationale: Responsible adoption combines evidence appraisal with curricular quality, contextual fit, equity, feasibility, professional learning, and an explicit evaluation plan.
choiceRationales: Correct. Responsible adoption combines evidence appraisal with curricular quality, contextual fit, equity, feasibility, professional learning, and an explicit evaluation plan.
Visual appeal does not indicate instructional quality, alignment, or evidence of effectiveness for the students who will use the materials.
Citations may describe general research rather than evidence for the specific program, so independent evaluation of quality is needed.
Programs depend on implementation capacity and learner fit, so ignoring local conditions increases the risk of poor results.

items.prompt: How should identifiable literacy data be shared?
choices: Share the data freely by email because every district employee works on behalf of students and needs full access to records.
Verify legitimate educational interest, FERPA and policy, consent, a secure method, and minimum information needed.
Remove the student’s name but keep other uniquely identifying details so colleagues can still understand the full context.
Post the literacy profile on the staff room bulletin board so all teachers can review it while planning their instruction.
items.rationale: Education records require role-based, purpose-limited, secure handling under current law and policy; professional curiosity is not the same as legitimate educational interest.
choiceRationales: District employment alone does not create a legitimate educational interest, so access must be limited to staff with an instructional role.
Correct. Education records require role-based, purpose-limited, secure handling under current law and policy; professional curiosity is not the same as legitimate educational interest.
Removing a name while keeping unique details can still identify the student, which fails to protect privacy as required by policy.
Posting identifiable data in a shared space exposes it to unauthorized people and violates privacy expectations for student records.

items.prompt: How should a specialist handle a financial conflict?
choices: Keep the financial relationship private because the program is popular with teachers and families.
Use student data in vendor marketing materials without authorization to help demonstrate results.
Disclose it, follow ethics and procurement rules, share objective evidence, and recuse if needed.
Guarantee specific student outcomes to administrators so the purchase decision can move forward.
items.rationale: Transparency and independent evidence protect students, schools, and professional trust when personal interests could influence recommendations.
choiceRationales: Hiding a financial interest undermines trust and violates ethics requirements, regardless of how popular the program may be locally.
Using student data in marketing without authorization violates privacy rules and professional ethics for handling education records.
Correct. Transparency and independent evidence protect students, schools, and professional trust when personal interests could influence recommendations.
Guaranteeing outcomes overstates evidence and compounds the conflict of interest rather than supporting an objective, transparent decision.

items.prompt: What makes literacy advocacy evidence based?
choices: Dismiss lived experience from students and families because it does not come from experimental research.
Promise decision makers that the proposed policy will help every student in the district equally.
Present only the evidence that supports the preferred position and omit findings that complicate it.
Combine student and family experience with disaggregated data, research quality, equity analysis, and review plans.
items.rationale: Responsible advocacy integrates multiple forms of evidence, identifies uncertainty and tradeoffs, centers affected communities, and includes a way to evaluate consequences.
choiceRationales: Lived experience provides important context about access and impact, complementing research rather than competing with it in advocacy.
Promising universal benefit overstates the evidence and leaves no room for monitoring or adjustment if outcomes differ across groups.
Omitting contrary findings weakens credibility and prevents decision makers from weighing the full range of evidence responsibly.
Correct. Responsible advocacy integrates multiple forms of evidence, identifies uncertainty and tradeoffs, centers affected communities, and includes a way to evaluate consequences.

items.prompt: A team asks whether literacy skills always emerge in a rigid sequence. What is the best response?
choices: Use the continuum to anticipate prerequisites while assessing each learner, not treating stages as fixed gates.
Expect every learner to master each continuum skill at the same chronological age before moving to new instruction.
Skip foundational word-level evidence whenever comprehension appears weak, since higher skills reveal lower ones.
Use current grade placement as the main indicator of instructional need and select materials only from that level.
items.rationale: Literacy components develop in related and partly overlapping ways; a continuum organizes assessment and instruction but does not erase individual, linguistic, cultural, disability, or opportunity differences.
choiceRationales: Correct. Literacy components develop in related and partly overlapping ways; a continuum organizes assessment and instruction but does not erase individual, linguistic, cultural, disability, or opportunity differences.
Literacy development follows broad patterns but varies widely; requiring identical ages for mastery ignores individual evidence and leads to mismatched instruction.
Weak comprehension can stem from word recognition, language, or knowledge gaps, so foundational evidence is needed to decide where instruction should begin.
Grade placement describes enrollment rather than demonstrated skill, so it cannot identify which components a reader has mastered or still needs to learn.

items.prompt: A student understands spoken explanations but cannot identify many printed words. What should the specialist investigate?
choices: Comprehension depends mainly on reading rate, so faster oral reading is the clearest sign that understanding is secure.
Comprehension depends on efficient word recognition and language comprehension, so each component should be assessed.
Strong listening comprehension makes decoding instruction unnecessary because readers can infer words from meaning.
Accurate word recognition by itself ensures text understanding once a reader can pronounce every printed word.
items.rationale: Word recognition and language comprehension make distinct, interacting contributions; instructional planning should locate the learner’s relative strengths and needs rather than infer one from the other.
choiceRationales: Rate is one fluency indicator; fast reading without adequate language comprehension or accuracy does not demonstrate that the reader understood the text.

Correct. Word recognition and language comprehension make distinct, interacting contributions; instructional planning should locate the learner’s relative strengths and needs rather than infer one from the other.
Listening comprehension cannot replace decoding, because readers must still translate print into words before language knowledge can build meaning.
Pronouncing words accurately is necessary but insufficient; vocabulary, syntax, background knowledge, and inference also determine whether text is understood.

items.prompt: Why should vocabulary, syntax, narrative, and listening comprehension be considered in a literacy evaluation?
choices: Oral-language evidence can replace direct assessment of print skills such as decoding, spelling, and word recognition.
Conversation samples establish a learner’s intelligence level, which then sets expectations for reading instruction.
Oral-language evidence helps explain meaning making and expression and guides language-rich instruction.
Oral-language assessment matters mainly before kindergarten and adds little once formal reading instruction begins.
items.rationale: Oral language supports vocabulary, syntax, discourse, inference, comprehension, and written expression across grades, but it must be integrated with direct print and writing evidence.
choiceRationales: Oral language and print skills are distinct components; strong speaking does not reveal whether a learner can decode or spell, so both need direct assessment.
Language samples describe vocabulary, syntax, and discourse use, but they are not intelligence measures and should not set fixed expectations for learners.
Correct. Oral language supports vocabulary, syntax, discourse, inference, comprehension, and written expression across grades, but it must be integrated with direct print and writing evidence.
Language comprehension continues to shape reading and writing across the elementary grades, so oral-language evidence remains useful after kindergarten.

items.prompt: Two students have the same comprehension score but different decoding and language patterns. What follows?
choices: Assign the same intervention to both students because their identical total scores indicate the same instructional need.
Assume both students have dyslexia because their composite reading scores fall below the expected benchmark range.
Select the lowest-grade workbook for both students so the materials match their shared overall performance level.
Analyze component skills and contexts separately, because an identical overall result can reflect distinct needs.
items.rationale: Composite performance can conceal different mechanisms; disaggregating word recognition, language, fluency, knowledge, writing, opportunity, and task conditions supports more precise instruction.
choiceRationales: Identical totals can hide different profiles, such as weak decoding with strong language or the reverse, so one intervention may miss each student’s need.
A low composite score does not establish dyslexia; a word-level difficulty must be documented with comprehensive evidence before any such conclusion is drawn.
Lowering materials for both students ignores their distinct component needs and can reduce access to grade-level vocabulary, knowledge, and complex ideas.

Correct. Composite performance can conceal different mechanisms; disaggregating word recognition, language, fluency, knowledge, writing, opportunity, and task conditions supports more precise instruction.

items.prompt: A learner has persistent difficulty reading unfamiliar words accurately and spelling despite appropriate instruction. What should the team consider?
choices: A word-level difficulty in accurate or fluent recognition, decoding, and encoding, evaluated comprehensively.
A visual disorder defined mainly by reversing letters and numbers when reading or writing beyond the first grade.
A reading problem caused primarily by low motivation, which improves once students receive engaging reading choices.
A comprehension difficulty that leaves word reading intact while making inferences and main ideas hard to identify.
items.rationale: Dyslexia is not established by reversals or a single score; evaluation considers persistent word-level patterns, instruction, language, development, functional impact, and exclusionary and co-occurring factors.
choiceRationales: Correct. Dyslexia is not established by reversals or a single score; evaluation considers persistent word-level patterns, instruction, language, development, functional impact, and exclusionary and co-occurring factors.
Letter reversals are common in early development and are not a defining feature of dyslexia, which centers on phonological and word-level reading difficulty.
Motivation can affect engagement, but dyslexia is not caused by low motivation; attributing it that way delays appropriate explicit word-level instruction.
A comprehension-only profile with intact decoding describes a different pattern; dyslexia primarily affects accurate or fluent word recognition and spelling.

items.prompt: A teacher attributes every reading error to slow processing. What should the specialist do?
choices: Treat a low processing-speed score as a complete reading diagnosis that explains the learner’s literacy difficulties.
Treat cognitive and behavioral factors as context while directly assessing literacy skills and response.
Set aside observable word-reading errors because attention and memory scores better explain the reading profile.
Delay literacy intervention until attention, memory, or processing speed improve enough to support new learning.
items.rationale: Attention, verbal memory, automaticity, processing speed, and graphomotor control can affect performance, but direct literacy evidence remains necessary for instructional and differential decisions.
choiceRationales: Processing speed may contribute to performance, but it cannot identify which literacy skills need instruction; direct reading and spelling evidence is still required.

Correct. Attention, verbal memory, automaticity, processing speed, and graphomotor control can affect performance, but direct literacy evidence remains necessary for instructional and differential decisions.
Observable word-reading errors are the most direct evidence of instructional need, and setting them aside in favor of cognitive scores weakens planning.
Waiting for cognitive change withholds effective literacy instruction; explicit teaching can proceed while attention and memory supports are provided.

items.prompt: A school uses unrelated activities across grades without a shared progression. What should the specialist recommend?
choices: Add more isolated skill worksheets each year without reviewing how they connect to standards or to prior instruction.
Use one commercial lesson script identically for every learner regardless of assessment evidence or language needs.
Align standards, skill progressions, texts, writing, assessment, and intervention so learning builds year to year.
Let each separate assessment define its own curriculum so teachers prepare students for every test format directly.
items.rationale: Coherence connects goals, content, instructional routines, assessment, intervention, materials, and grade-to-grade development while allowing responsive adaptation.
choiceRationales: Adding unconnected worksheets increases activity without building a coherent progression, leaving gaps and redundancies across grade levels.
A single script applied identically ignores evidence about learner needs and language access, so it cannot provide coherent differentiated instruction.
Correct. Coherence connects goals, content, instructional routines, assessment, intervention, materials, and grade-to-grade development while allowing responsive adaptation.
Letting each test dictate content fragments the curriculum and narrows instruction to formats rather than to coherent standards-based skill development.

items.prompt: A multilingual learner uses knowledge from a home language while reading English. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Ask learners to set aside their home language during literacy lessons so English acquisition can progress faster.
Interpret each cross-language feature in a learner’s English as possible evidence of a reading or language disability.
Avoid culturally familiar texts during instruction because familiarity reduces the rigor of comprehension tasks.
Treat linguistic and cultural repertoires as assets while teaching new English forms and monitoring growth.
items.rationale: Asset-based instruction connects prior knowledge and cross-linguistic resources with explicit teaching of English language and literacy, without confusing difference, opportunity, and disability.
choiceRationales: Discouraging the home language removes a resource for transfer and vocabulary, and it can harm identity and engagement without speeding English growth.
Cross-language features are typical in English development; treating them as disability evidence risks misidentification and inappropriate services.
Culturally familiar texts can support access and engagement while still carrying rigorous vocabulary, structure, and inference demands for comprehension.

Correct. Asset-based instruction connects prior knowledge and cross-linguistic resources with explicit teaching of English language and literacy, without confusing difference, opportunity, and disability.

items.prompt: A teacher asks whether syllable blending and phoneme deletion measure the same level of sound awareness. What is correct?
choices: Phonological awareness spans spoken units such as syllables and rimes; phonemic awareness targets individual phonemes.
Both phonological and phonemic awareness require printed letters, so neither can be practiced through oral activities.
Phonics is the broader oral category, and phonological awareness is one narrower part of letter-sound instruction.
Phonemic awareness concerns the meanings of words, while phonological awareness concerns how sentences are built.
items.rationale: Phonological awareness includes words, syllables, onset-rime, and phonemes; phonemic awareness is the most specific level and can be practiced orally before or alongside graphemes.
choiceRationales: Correct. Phonological awareness includes words, syllables, onset-rime, and phonemes; phonemic awareness is the most specific level and can be practiced orally before or alongside graphemes.
Both forms of awareness operate on spoken language and can be taught orally; print is added deliberately later to connect sounds with letters.
Phonics links sounds to print, so it is not an oral category; phonological awareness is the broader spoken-language skill set rather than a subset of phonics.
Phonemic awareness concerns individual speech sounds, not meaning; word meaning belongs to vocabulary, and sentence construction belongs to syntax.

items.prompt: A student is asked to say every sound in “ship.” Which skill is being assessed?
choices: Combining a sequence of spoken phonemes into a whole word, such as hearing /s/ /u/ /n/ and saying sun.
Separating a spoken word into each of its individual phonemes, such as saying /m/ /a/ /p/ for map.
Naming each printed letter in a written word in order, such as reading the letters m, a, p aloud from a card.
Identifying the meaning of a morpheme within a word, such as explaining that un- in unhappy means not.
items.rationale: Segmentation requires identifying the sequence of phonemes in a spoken word; the number of sounds need not equal the number of printed letters.
choiceRationales: Combining phonemes into a word is blending, the reverse operation; segmentation requires breaking the spoken word apart into its separate sounds.
Correct. Segmentation requires identifying the sequence of phonemes in a spoken word; the number of sounds need not equal the number of printed letters.
Naming printed letters assesses letter knowledge with visible print, whereas phoneme segmentation is an oral task that requires hearing individual sounds.
Explaining a prefix meaning assesses morphological knowledge and vocabulary, not the ability to isolate and separate the sounds within a spoken word.

items.prompt: A learner changes the first sound in “map” to /s/ and says “sap.” What skill is demonstrated?
choices: Print-directionality knowledge, such as tracking text from left to right and returning to the next line correctly.
Counting the syllables in multisyllable spoken words by clapping each beat without isolating individual sounds.
Phoneme substitution, such as changing the /k/ in cat to /h/ to say hat, which is a form of phoneme manipulation.
Sorting picture cards into vocabulary categories such as animals, foods, and tools based on their meanings.
items.rationale: Deleting, adding, or substituting phonemes requires deliberate manipulation of the sound sequence and is more complex than recognition alone.
choiceRationales: Print directionality is a concept-of-print skill about how text is arranged on a page, not an operation that changes individual sounds in spoken words.
Syllable counting works at a larger sound unit and does not require learners to isolate, delete, or substitute individual phonemes within words.
Correct. Deleting, adding, or substituting phonemes requires deliberate manipulation of the sound sequence and is more complex than recognition alone.
Sorting pictures by meaning builds vocabulary and categorization, but it does not require any manipulation of the speech sounds within words.

items.prompt: What understanding allows a beginning reader to connect spoken words with printed words?
choices: Every letter in English represents exactly one sound, so each word can be decoded letter by letter in sequence.
Word meaning can be derived from the visual shape of the letters, so readers rely mainly on word outlines.
Print is learned as whole visual pictures, so each new word is memorized separately from letter-sound knowledge.
Letters and letter patterns represent the phonemes of oral language in systematic, learnable ways.
items.rationale: The alphabetic principle links phonology and orthography; English correspondences vary, so teaching progresses from common transparent patterns to more complex ones.
choiceRationales: English letters and patterns often represent more than one sound, so the alphabetic principle describes systematic relationships rather than one-to-one mapping.
Word shapes are unreliable cues; skilled readers attend to letters and their sound relationships, which the alphabetic principle explicitly describes.
Memorizing words as pictures bypasses the sound-letter system the alphabetic principle describes and limits independent reading of unfamiliar words.
Correct. The alphabetic principle links phonology and orthography; English correspondences vary, so teaching progresses from common transparent patterns to more complex ones.

items.prompt: A child points to the first word, tracks left to right, and distinguishes a letter from a word. What is being developed?
choices: Understanding how print works in books, such as directionality, spacing between words, and book parts.
Analyzing advanced morphological structure, such as identifying Greek and Latin roots in academic vocabulary.
Measuring silent-reading rate on grade-level passages to estimate how quickly students process connected text.
Interpreting norm-referenced scores to compare a learner’s reading performance with a national reference group.
items.rationale: Concepts of print include directionality, word boundaries, book handling, and distinctions among letters, words, and sentences that support access to alphabetic instruction.
choiceRationales: Correct. Concepts of print include directionality, word boundaries, book handling, and distinctions among letters, words, and sentences that support access to alphabetic instruction.
Root analysis is an advanced word-study skill for morphology and vocabulary, not the foundational understanding of how books and print work.
Silent-reading rate measures fluency on connected text, whereas concepts of print concern basic knowledge such as directionality and word boundaries.
Norm-referenced interpretation is an assessment practice for comparing scores, not a learner skill about how print is organized and functions.

items.prompt: A specialist adds grapheme tiles after students can blend sounds orally. What is the rationale?
choices: Adding letters converts phonemic-awareness practice into vocabulary instruction focused mainly on word meanings.
Connecting phonemes with graphemes can strengthen transfer from oral sound awareness to decoding and spelling.
Oral sound awareness must be fully completed before any print is introduced, so letters should be delayed.
Using letter tiles removes the need for explicit teacher feedback because the tiles show learners their errors.
items.rationale: Sound awareness and letter–sound knowledge are mutually supportive; carefully linking them helps students apply phonemic skills to reading and encoding.
choiceRationales: Letters connect sounds to print for decoding and spelling; they do not shift the activity toward word meanings, which is the focus of vocabulary work.
Correct. Sound awareness and letter–sound knowledge are mutually supportive; carefully linking them helps students apply phonemic skills to reading and encoding.
Research supports linking sounds and letters once oral tasks are understood, so delaying all print can slow transfer to reading and spelling.
Manipulatives support practice, but learners still need explicit modeling and corrective feedback to connect phonemes accurately with graphemes.

items.prompt: Students can recognize rhyme but cannot blend or segment phonemes. What next step is most defensible?
choices: Begin phonological instruction with advanced Latin roots so learners meet complex academic words early on.
Assign independent silent reading as the main activity because exposure to print develops phonological skills.
Model explicitly, moving from larger units toward blending, segmenting, and manipulating sounds using data.
Repeat rhyme-identification games indefinitely without monitoring whether learners progress to phoneme work.
items.rationale: Instruction should be explicit, cumulative, responsive, and focused on the skills needed for word reading rather than tied mechanically to one universal sequence.
choiceRationales: Latin roots belong to later morphological study and do not address the spoken sound structures that phonological awareness instruction targets.
Silent reading does not provide explicit modeling or practice with spoken sound units, so it cannot replace systematic phonological instruction.
Correct. Instruction should be explicit, cumulative, responsive, and focused on the skills needed for word reading rather than tied mechanically to one universal sequence.
Rhyming is an early skill; repeating it without monitoring prevents learners from advancing to phoneme-level blending and segmenting they need.

items.prompt: A coach observes a lesson asking students to name printed letter–sound correspondences but calls it phonemic awareness. How should the coach respond?
choices: Phonics concerns comprehension strategies, while phonological awareness concerns how well students decode text.
Phonemic awareness always relies on written words, so the two terms differ only in how many letters are shown.
The terms are interchangeable in every instructional context, so the distinction does not affect lesson planning.
Phonological and phonemic awareness concern spoken sounds; phonics explicitly connects those sounds with print.
items.rationale: Clear construct labels help teams select aligned assessments and instruction: oral sound analysis is distinct from, though closely related to, print–sound mapping.
choiceRationales: Phonics teaches letter-sound relationships for decoding and spelling; comprehension strategies are a separate component of reading instruction.
Phonemic awareness is an oral skill that can be practiced without print, so describing it as dependent on written words confuses it with phonics.
Treating the terms as interchangeable blurs instructional goals; teachers need to know whether a lesson targets spoken sounds or sound-letter links.
Correct. Clear construct labels help teams select aligned assessments and instruction: oral sound analysis is distinct from, though closely related to, print–sound mapping.

items.prompt: Students are learning a common vowel correspondence. Which lesson design is strongest?
choices: Teach the sound–spelling link explicitly, guide blending and spelling, then apply it in words and connected text.
Ask students to infer the new pattern from an unrelated story during independent reading without teacher guidance.
Have students memorize written definitions of the phonics rule and recite them before any word-reading practice.
Introduce several conflicting spelling exceptions first so students see the full complexity before the main pattern.
items.rationale: Explicit explanation, cumulative practice, corrective feedback, spelling, and connected-text application help students establish and generalize a new correspondence.
choiceRationales: Correct. Explicit explanation, cumulative practice, corrective feedback, spelling, and connected-text application help students establish and generalize a new correspondence.
Incidental discovery from an unrelated text leaves many readers without a clear model, so the pattern may never be learned accurately or applied reliably.
Reciting rule definitions does not build blending, spelling, or transfer to text; students need guided practice with real words and connected reading.
Leading with exceptions creates confusion before the common pattern is secure; explicit instruction establishes the high-utility pattern first.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a passage closely aligned with recently taught correspondences?
choices: It keeps beginning readers in one controlled text type for the rest of the elementary grades to build confidence.
It offers many chances to apply newly learned decoding patterns accurately while reading connected text.
It measures listening comprehension without print so teachers can separate language skills from decoding.
It replaces read-alouds and knowledge-building discussions because controlled text covers those goals as well.
items.rationale: Aligned decodable text supports transfer and accuracy while a complete literacy program also includes rich oral language, diverse texts, vocabulary, knowledge, and writing.
choiceRationales: Decodable text is a temporary bridge for practicing new patterns; it is not intended to limit readers to one text type throughout the elementary years.
Correct. Aligned decodable text supports transfer and accuracy while a complete literacy program also includes rich oral language, diverse texts, vocabulary, knowledge, and writing.
Decodable passages require reading print, so they assess and practice decoding rather than listening comprehension, which is measured without text.
Read-alouds build vocabulary, knowledge, and language comprehension that controlled texts cannot supply, so both belong in a complete literacy block.

items.prompt: A frequently encountered word contains both regular and unexpected spellings. What should the teacher emphasize?
choices: Treat every letter in an irregular word as arbitrary so students learn the full word as one unanalyzed unit.
Require visual memorization from flash cards without any analysis of the sounds represented by the letters.
Map predictable sound-letter parts, flag the unusual part, and connect pronunciation with meaning.
Avoid teaching the word until students have learned every exception pattern that could appear in later texts.
items.rationale: Analyzing what is regular and what is unusual supports orthographic learning more precisely than presenting the entire word as a visual shape.
choiceRationales: Most irregular words contain regular sound-letter parts, so treating every letter as arbitrary discards information that supports durable memory.
